lesson.title: The People's Party: Farmers Rise Against the Railroads and Banks
lesson.summary: In the early 1890s, indebted and angry farmers built a new political party, the Populists, to challenge the railroads, banks, and Gilded Age elites they blamed for their economic collapse.
lesson.body:
After the Civil War, farmers across the Great Plains and the South faced a slow economic squeeze. Crop prices for wheat, corn, and cotton kept falling as American farms flooded a global market, while the money supply, tied to a limited gold standard, did not grow to match it. That combination produced deflation: the same debts farmers had taken on to buy land, seed, and equipment became harder to pay off every year, because the dollars they owed were worth more than the dollars they had borrowed. Many farmers fell into a cycle of debt they could not escape.

Railroads made the squeeze worse. The rail lines that had opened the Plains to settlement, often built with enormous government land grants, frequently charged farmers steep and sometimes discriminatory freight rates to move crops to market, especially in regions where a single company controlled the only line. Farmers had no leverage against a monopoly they could not do without. At the same time, industrial workers organizing in this same period, through groups like the Knights of Labor, were making similar complaints about concentrated corporate power, and Populist leaders hoped to build a coalition that united aggrieved farmers and aggrieved wage workers against what they saw as a shared enemy.

Farmers had already begun organizing economically through cooperative groups, most importantly the Farmers' Alliance, which spread rapidly across the South and Plains in the 1870s and 1880s. By the end of the 1880s, many Alliance leaders concluded that cooperative buying and selling alone could not fix problems rooted in national monetary and railroad policy, and that only direct political power would work. That conclusion led to the founding of the People's Party, commonly called the Populists, at a national convention in Omaha, Nebraska, in July 1892.

The party's Omaha Platform laid out a sweeping set of demands: free and unlimited coinage of silver alongside gold, a graduated income tax, direct popular election of United States senators (who were still chosen by state legislatures), government ownership of the railroads and telegraph lines, a subtreasury system to give farmers access to low interest crop loans, and an eight hour workday, a plank aimed directly at winning labor's support.

In the 1892 presidential election, Populist candidate James B. Weaver won over a million popular votes and 22 electoral votes, carrying several western states outright, the strongest showing by any third party since before the Civil War. The party also elected members of Congress and state officials across the Plains and South. Many Populist ideas outlived the party itself: a federal income tax and the direct election of senators both became constitutional amendments in 1913, and Populist critiques of concentrated corporate power echoed for decades in the Progressive and New Deal reforms that followed.
